quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — How Python Runs and Stores Data
quizzes.intro: Confirm the basics: interpreters, values, types, variables, and simple expressions.

questions.prompt: What does the Python interpreter do?

options.text: It designs your program goals automatically
It reads Python instructions and executes them
It only checks spelling in comments
It converts every program into a website

questions.explanation: The interpreter reads Python source and carries out the instructions on your machine.

wrongExplanations.a: You still define goals and logic; the interpreter executes what you write.
wrongExplanations.c: Comments are ignored; the interpreter executes statements and expressions.
wrongExplanations.d: Python can build many kinds of programs, not only websites.

options.text: True

questions.explanation: 3.14 without quotes is a floating-point number. Quoted text is a string.

wrongExplanations.a: Quotes make it a string, not a float.

questions.prompt: After `score = 10` then `score = score + 5`, what does `score` refer to?

options.text: "score + 5"
None

questions.explanation: Assignment evaluates the right-hand side and rebinds the name. 10 + 5 yields 15.

wrongExplanations.a: The second assignment replaces the old binding.
wrongExplanations.c: Python stores the computed value, not the unevaluated text.
wrongExplanations.d: The name still refers to a number, not None.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `20 / 4` in Python 3?
questions.explanation: True division with `/` returns a float, so 20 / 4 is 5.0.

wrongExplanations.a: That would be an int; `/` yields a float in Python 3.
wrongExplanations.c: Division returns a number, not a string.
wrongExplanations.d: 4 would be incorrect arithmetic for 20 divided by 4.

options.text: Because 30 is too large
Because Python cannot concatenate str and int with +
Because Age is a reserved keyword
Because print was not used

questions.explanation: Convert with str(30) or use an f-string. + does not automatically mix text and integers.

wrongExplanations.a: Size is irrelevant here; types are the issue.
wrongExplanations.d: The expression is invalid even before printing.

questions.prompt: If `a = [1, 2]` and `b = a`, then `b.append(3)`, what is `a`?

options.text: Error: lists cannot be shared

questions.explanation: a and b refer to the same list object, so an in-place append is visible through both names.

wrongExplanations.a: That would be true only if b were a separate copy.
wrongExplanations.c: Append adds to the existing list; it does not replace it with [3].
wrongExplanations.d: Python allows multiple names to reference one mutable object.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Decisions and Loops
quizzes.intro: Check your understanding of conditionals, boolean logic, and repetition patterns.

questions.prompt: In an if/elif/else chain, which block runs?

options.text: Every block whose condition is True
Only the first matching block, then the chain stops
Only the else block
A random matching block

questions.explanation: Python checks top to bottom and executes the first matching branch in the chain.

wrongExplanations.a: Unlike separate independent if statements, elif/else are mutually exclusive in one chain.
wrongExplanations.c: else runs only when no previous condition matched.
wrongExplanations.d: Control flow is deterministic, not random.

questions.explanation: range(3) produces 0, 1, and 2. The end is exclusive and the default start is 0.

wrongExplanations.c: 3 is not included because the stop value is exclusive.
wrongExplanations.d: range does not reverse unless you set a negative step.

questions.prompt: Which loop is usually best when you do not know how many retries input validation will need?

options.text: A for loop over range(0)
A while loop that breaks on valid input
An else-only chain with no loop
A list literal

questions.explanation: while is ideal when repetition depends on a condition that becomes true at an unknown time.

wrongExplanations.c: Without a loop you cannot retry repeatedly.
wrongExplanations.d: A list stores values; it does not repeat logic by itself.

options.text: Deleting all variables at the end of a program
Initializing a value, then updating it as you loop over items
Printing every line twice
Converting all strings to booleans

questions.explanation: Examples include totaling scores, counting matches, or building a new list item by item.

wrongExplanations.c: Printing twice is not the accumulator idea.
wrongExplanations.d: Type conversion is a different concept.

questions.prompt: What does `continue` do inside a loop?

options.text: Ends the entire program
Skips the rest of the current iteration and goes to the next one
Deletes the loop variable forever
Converts the loop into a function

questions.explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration. break, by contrast, exits the loop entirely.

wrongExplanations.a: continue does not terminate the program.
wrongExplanations.c: The loop variable is not deleted forever.
wrongExplanations.d: Functions are defined with def, not continue.

options.text: Treats the empty list as falsey and skips the if block
Always enters the if block
Raises IndexError immediately
Creates a new list with one None

questions.explanation: Empty lists are falsey in boolean context, so the if body is skipped.

wrongExplanations.b: Non-empty lists are truthy; empty lists are not.
wrongExplanations.c: A boolean check on an empty list does not index it.
wrongExplanations.d: The condition does not mutate the list.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Functions, Errors, and Program Thinking
quizzes.intro: Bring it together: functions, returns, scope, debugging, and small-program design.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between printing a value inside a function and returning it?

options.text: They are identical in all cases
print shows output to humans; return hands a value back to the caller for further use
return can only send strings
print stores the value in a global constant automatically

questions.explanation: If you need the result later in the program, return it. Printing alone leaves the caller with None unless something is returned.

wrongExplanations.a: They serve different purposes and produce different caller behavior.
wrongExplanations.c: Functions can return any object type.
wrongExplanations.d: print does not create globals for you.

questions.prompt: A variable assigned inside a function is usually:

options.text: Local to that function call
Automatically available everywhere in every file
Deleted from memory before the function starts
Required to be uppercase

questions.explanation: Local scope keeps functions from accidentally interfering with each other. Pass inputs in and return outputs out.

wrongExplanations.b: That describes global behavior, which is not the default for assignments inside functions.
wrongExplanations.c: The variable exists during the function execution.
wrongExplanations.d: Uppercase is only a convention for constants, not a language requirement for locals.

questions.prompt: You see `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.2'`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: int() cannot parse '3.2' because of the decimal point
Python forbids all numbers
The variable name int is missing
You must use print before int

questions.explanation: Use float('3.2') if you need a decimal, or validate/reject non-integers if only whole numbers are allowed.

wrongExplanations.c: int here is the built-in converter, not a missing variable definition of that kind.
wrongExplanations.d: print is unrelated to conversion success.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first debugging step when a traceback appears?

options.text: Delete the whole file and rewrite from memory
Read the error type/message and jump to the reported line
Ignore the traceback and keep adding features
Wrap everything in a bare except: pass

questions.explanation: Tracebacks are diagnostic maps. Start with the final error and line number, then inspect related values.

wrongExplanations.a: Total rewrites waste information the traceback already gave you.
wrongExplanations.c: Adding features on a broken base creates more failures.
wrongExplanations.d: Swallowing all errors hides problems and makes debugging harder.

questions.prompt: Which function best follows a clear contract for beginners?

options.text: A function named x that prints random things and also edits globals
def average(scores): returns the mean of a non-empty numeric list (or errors clearly if empty)
A function with no name that runs only when Python feels ready
A function that requires the caller to guess whether it prints or returns

questions.explanation: Clear names, explicit inputs/outputs, and defined empty-input behavior make functions testable and reusable.

wrongExplanations.a: Vague names and hidden side effects create fragile code.
wrongExplanations.c: Functions must be defined with names (unless using specialized anonymous forms intentionally).
wrongExplanations.d: Callers should not have to guess the interface.

questions.prompt: Before writing code for a tiny utility, what professional habit helps most?

options.text: Write two sample inputs/outputs and note edge cases in plain English
Choose the longest possible variable names with no plan
Avoid running the program until it is 500 lines long
Start by optimizing for million-row performance only

questions.explanation: Examples and edge cases clarify the goal. Then implement thinly, test, and refactor.

wrongExplanations.b: Names matter, but planning matters first.
wrongExplanations.c: Frequent small runs catch errors early.
wrongExplanations.d: Beginners should prioritize correctness and clarity before premature optimization.

questions.prompt: In the flashcard quizzer design, why store each card as a dictionary with prompt and answer?

options.text: Because dictionaries are the only type Python allows
Because related fields stay together as one record, reducing parallel-list bugs
Because dictionaries cannot be looped over
Because input() requires dictionaries

questions.explanation: Keeping related fields together is a core data-modeling habit as programs grow beyond single values.

wrongExplanations.a: Python has many types; dictionaries are one useful choice for records.
wrongExplanations.c: Dictionaries are commonly iterated with keys/values/items.
wrongExplanations.d: input() returns a string; it does not require dictionary cards.
